title: Is the Banach-space measure of dependence always equivalent to alpha or to beta?
statement: For a real Banach space B define R^B_{inf,inf}(A,C) = sup |E<X,Y> - <EX,EY>| / (|| ||X||_B ||_inf || ||Y||_{B*} ||_inf) over simple B-valued A-measurable X and B*-valued C-measurable Y. Two measures of dependence are equivalent if each becomes arbitrarily small as the other becomes sufficiently small. It is known that R^H is equivalent to alpha for any nontrivial Hilbert space H (Dehling-Philipp), and that R^B = 2 beta for B = l_inf, l_1 and c_0. For an arbitrary nontrivial real Banach space B, is R^B always equivalent to one of alpha or beta?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 'Bradley strong mixing conditions survey open questions solved' returned the survey itself (Probab. Surveys 2 (2005) 107-144) on Project Euclid, EuDML, Semantic Scholar and arXiv math/0511078, plus later papers citing it (subgeometric ergodicity and beta-mixing, INAR mixing); none addressed the Banach-space dependence measure R^B. No evidence of resolution.

attempt.method: Read the two known endpoints as a local-Banach-space statement. Hilbert space gives alpha; l_1, l_inf and c_0 give exactly 2 beta. These are the extreme cases of type and cotype, so conjecture that the dichotomy is governed by B-convexity (equivalently, by whether B contains l_1^n uniformly, by the Giesy-James theorem).
attempt.result: The conjecture I can state precisely is: R^B is equivalent to beta if B contains l_1^n uniformly (B not B-convex), and equivalent to alpha otherwise. The 'if' half has a mechanism: the construction of [47, Theorem 3.1] giving R^B = 2 beta for l_1 uses only that the unit ball of B contains an almost-isometric copy of the l_1^n ball on which the covariance form can be made to compute the total variation distance between the joint law and the product law, which is exactly beta; a uniform l_1^n embedding is enough to run it up to an arbitrarily small loss, which is all that 'equivalence' requires. The 'only if' half would follow from a Maurey-Pisier type statement transferred to the bilinear covariance form. Note also that the question presupposes a dichotomy: since beta is strictly stronger than alpha, a third equivalence class strictly between them is not excluded a priori, and I could not exclude it.
attempt.obstruction: Transferring Maurey-Pisier is the wall: the covariance bilinear form is evaluated on SIMPLE random variables with the sup-norm normalisation, so what is needed is a finite-dimensional statement about the norm of the covariance form on B_n x B_n* for finite-dimensional subspaces B_n, with constants depending only on the type/cotype constants. I have no such estimate, and the known interpolation-theoretic comparisons in the references of the source are for the specific coefficients alpha, beta, rho, phi rather than for a general B.
attempt.key_identity: Hilbert: R^H equivalent to alpha; l_1, l_inf, c_0: R^B = 2 beta; conjectured dichotomy by B-convexity (uniform containment of l_1^n).

title: Does phi-mixing imply rho*-mixing?
statement: If a given (strictly stationary) random sequence is phi-mixing, does it follow that it is rho*-mixing? The author conjectured yes; Walter Philipp thought the answer negative. A positive answer would give the Ibragimov CLT conjecture and the Iosifescu invariance-principle conjecture for phi-mixing sequences with divergent variance.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 'Bradley strong mixing conditions survey open questions solved phi-mixing implies rho*-mixing counterexample' returned only the survey itself in several repositories and unrelated later mixing papers; nothing announcing a proof or a counterexample. No evidence of resolution.

attempt.method: Compare the two-sided (past/future) and interlaced settings. The classical Cogburn-Ibragimov inequality rho(A,C) <= 2 phi(A,C)^{1/2} holds for ANY two sigma-fields, so the whole question is whether phi-mixing of the past/future pairs forces smallness of phi (or of rho) for INTERLACED pairs, i.e. whether phi(n) -> 0 implies phi*(n) -> 0.
attempt.result: The reduction is exact: since rho <= 2 phi^{1/2} for arbitrary pairs of sigma-fields, phi*(n) -> 0 implies rho*(n) -> 0, so a positive answer to Question 2 would follow from 'phi-mixing implies phi*-mixing'. Conversely a counterexample must have phi(n) -> 0 with rho*(n) bounded away from 0, and by the survey's Theorem 4.5 the coefficients rho and rho* can be prescribed essentially arbitrarily and independently for stationary sequences, which is exactly the kind of freedom a counterexample needs; that freedom is why I regard Philipp's negative expectation as the better bet. What blocks the direct construction is that Theorem 4.5 prescribes alpha, rho and rho* but says nothing about phi, and the survey records that no comparable exactness result is known for phi (this is the content of Question 7, recorded here as D0035).
attempt.obstruction: The concrete wall is the missing exactness/prescription theorem for phi. The Kesten-O'Brien style constructions realise prescribed rates for alpha, rho, rho*; to build a counterexample one needs a construction that simultaneously forces phi(n) -> 0 (a strong, conditional-probability-uniform requirement) and keeps a fixed interlaced correlation, and the conditional-probability uniformity of phi is precisely what the cutting-and-stacking constructions do not control.
attempt.key_identity: rho(A,C) <= 2 phi(A,C)^{1/2} for any two sigma-fields, so phi* -> 0 implies rho* -> 0; the question is whether phi -> 0 implies phi* -> 0.

title: A rho-mixing, bilaterally deterministic, finite-state stationary sequence
statement: Does there exist a nondegenerate strictly stationary, finite-state, rho-mixing, bilaterally deterministic sequence X = (X_k, k in Z)? (Bilaterally deterministic: the sequence is measurable with respect to its double tail sigma-field, modulo null sets.)
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 as for D0030; the survey is the most recent statement found and no construction or impossibility proof appeared. No evidence of resolution.

attempt.method: Separate what rho-mixing does and does not force. rho(n) -> 0 forces triviality of the ordinary tail sigma-field (a rho-mixing sequence is mixing in the ergodic-theoretic sense, hence has trivial tail by Kolmogorov-type arguments), but bilateral determinism is a statement about the DOUBLE tail, which can be everything even for very strongly mixing sequences.
attempt.result: The known bilaterally deterministic examples with strong mixing are built by cutting-and-stacking with an intricate coding that reconstructs the middle of a word from the two far ends. The obstruction to making them rho-mixing can be localised: rho-mixing means the correlation of ANY two square-integrable functions of past and future decays, and for a finite-state sequence the space of such functions is spanned by cylinder indicators, so rho(n) -> 0 forces sup over cylinder pairs of the normalised covariance to vanish. Bilateral determinism, on the other hand, produces a sequence of pairs (f_m, g_m) -- the two far ends of a word -- whose joint function determines the middle symbol exactly; the correlation of X_0 with the pair (f_m, g_m) is therefore bounded below uniformly in m. That does NOT immediately contradict rho(n) -> 0, because the pair straddles the origin rather than sitting in a past/future pair separated by n. So the two properties are compatible at the level of this argument, and the question is genuinely about whether the reconstruction can be arranged with a correlation that is spread thinly over many cylinders.
attempt.obstruction: The wall is quantitative: rho-mixing forbids any single normalised pair of past/future functions with correlation bounded below, but the reconstruction map is a function of the WHOLE double tail, and there is no known way to extract from it a single past/future pair with a non-vanishing normalised correlation. An impossibility proof would need such an extraction; a construction would need a cutting-and-stacking scheme with quantitative rho decay, and the existing schemes (which give strong mixing) have rho(n) = 1 for all n because the marker structure creates a bounded pair of indicator functions with correlation bounded below.
attempt.key_identity: rho(n) -> 0 forbids a normalised past/future pair with correlation bounded below; bilateral determinism only produces a straddling pair.

title: Ornstein's problem: is a strongly mixing finite-state process isomorphic to a Bernoulli shift?
statement: Suppose X = (X_k, k in Z) is a strictly stationary, finite-state, strongly mixing (alpha(n) -> 0) random sequence. Does it follow that X is isomorphic to a Bernoulli shift? The question remains open even with strong mixing replaced by rho-mixing or rho*-mixing; Martin and Strittmatter proved it under a sufficiently fast rate of convergence of alpha(n) to 0.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 'strictly stationary finite-state strongly mixing isomorphic to Bernoulli shift open question solved' returned the survey (arXiv math/0511078, Duke and Project Euclid copies), Bradley's Encyclopedia of Mathematics entry, and Penn State's 'Finite-state, stationary, phi-mixing processes which are not very weak Bernoulli with rate O(1/n)'. The search summary states explicitly that the question, posed by Ornstein in the 1970s, remains unsolved and that only rate-restricted positive results (Martin, Strittmatter) exist. Open.

attempt.method: Use Ornstein's criterion: X is isomorphic to a Bernoulli shift iff it is very weak Bernoulli (VWB). So the question is whether alpha(n) -> 0 implies VWB for finite-state processes.
attempt.result: The gap can be stated as a rate gap and that is the honest summary. VWB requires the conditional law of (X_1,...,X_n) given the past to be within dbar-distance eps of the unconditional law, for n large, and the standard route bounds dbar by a sum of the mixing coefficients over a window of length n, which needs sum-type control, i.e. a rate. The Penn State result found in the status search (finite-state phi-mixing processes that are not VWB with rate O(1/n)) shows the rate cannot be improved for free even under phi-mixing, so the residual question is genuinely about qualitative alpha(n) -> 0 with no rate. My reading: an affirmative answer would have to produce a dbar estimate that is not a sum of mixing coefficients, i.e. an argument using the finiteness of the state space to convert a qualitative decorrelation into a coupling; no such mechanism is known.
attempt.obstruction: The concrete wall: dbar-distance is not controlled by any single mixing coefficient without a rate, because dbar is a per-coordinate average of a coupling cost over a window of length n, and n mixing coefficients each of size alpha(m) can sum to something of order n alpha(m) which is useless unless alpha decays. Converting decorrelation into coupling without a rate would need a compactness/limiting argument in the space of processes, and the class of strongly mixing finite-state processes is not compact in dbar.
attempt.key_identity: Ornstein: isomorphic to a Bernoulli shift iff very weak Bernoulli; the missing step is a rate-free dbar estimate.

title: Does phi-mixing imply rho*-mixing for Markov chains?
statement: If a given Markov chain is phi-mixing, does it follow that it is rho*-mixing? (The Markov-chain special case of Question 2. Examples are known of a stationary countable-state Markov chain that is rho-mixing but not rho*-mixing, and of a stationary chain that is rho*-mixing but not absolutely regular.)
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 as for D0030; nothing found on the Markov special case beyond the survey. No evidence of resolution.

attempt.method: Exploit the Markov property. For a Markov chain, phi-mixing is equivalent to a Doeblin-type condition (by Theorem 3.3(2) of the source, phi(n) < 1/2 for some n forces exponential decay), so under the hypothesis the chain is uniformly ergodic. Then try to reduce the interlaced coefficient rho*(n) to a product over the gaps between the blocks of the two interlaced index sets.
attempt.result: The reduction works block by block and identifies exactly where it fails. Let S and T be interlaced index sets with all gaps at least n. Order the blocks along Z; by the Markov property, conditionally on the variables in any one gap, the configuration to the left is independent of the configuration to the right. Uniform ergodicity gives, for each gap, a total-variation contraction by a factor at most phi(n). If there were only ONE gap, rho over that gap would be at most 2 phi(n)^{1/2}, giving the result. With k gaps, the naive bound multiplies k contraction factors but the functions involved are not products, so one only gets a bound of the form min(1, k * something) rather than a product, and the supremum defining rho* is over all k.
attempt.obstruction: The wall is the unbounded number of blocks: rho*(n) takes a supremum over ALL pairs of interlaced index sets, hence over arbitrarily many alternations, and each alternation can contribute a fresh correlation of size comparable to rho(n) even if each individual gap is strongly decoupling. This is exactly the mechanism behind the known example (reference [36] of the source) of a stationary countable-state Markov chain that is rho-mixing but not rho*-mixing, so the Markov property alone cannot close the gap; what is needed is that phi-mixing, unlike rho-mixing, controls conditional probabilities uniformly and therefore might survive the alternations. Making that precise requires a multi-gap version of the Cogburn-Ibragimov inequality, which I do not have.
attempt.key_identity: One gap: rho <= 2 phi(n)^{1/2} by Cogburn-Ibragimov plus the Markov property; the supremum over arbitrarily many alternations is what is uncontrolled.

title: A psi-mixing or 1-dependent sequence that is not a function of a Harris recurrent Markov chain
statement: Does there exist a strictly stationary psi-mixing (or perhaps even 1-dependent) sequence which cannot be represented as an instantaneous function of a strictly stationary, Harris recurrent Markov chain?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 as for D0030; the survey is the most recent statement found. Related literature on 1-dependent processes that are not 1-block or 2-block factors of i.i.d. sequences (Aaronson, Gilat, Keane, de Valk; Burton, Goulet, Meester) exists but addresses a different representation class. No evidence of resolution.

attempt.method: Compare the two representation classes. An instantaneous function of a stationary Harris recurrent chain has a regeneration structure: the chain hits a small set infinitely often and the excursions between successive regeneration times are i.i.d. So such a process is a 'renewal-block' process. The question is therefore whether every psi-mixing (or 1-dependent) stationary process admits such a regeneration.
attempt.result: The right invariant to look at is the regeneration structure, and it gives a concrete route to a negative answer. If X is an instantaneous function of a Harris recurrent chain, then X is a block factor of an i.i.d. sequence in the weak sense that it decomposes into i.i.d. blocks of random length with a geometric-type tail (under uniform ergodicity, exponential). 1-dependent processes are known NOT all to be 1-block factors of i.i.d. sequences: the Aaronson-Gilat-Keane-de Valk example is a 1-dependent 3-state process that is not a 1-block factor. That example is the natural candidate here, and the honest statement is that the question reduces to whether it (or a variant) admits any regeneration at all. My attempt at the reduction found no obstruction to regeneration for that particular example, so a genuinely new construction is likely needed.
attempt.obstruction: The wall is that the Harris class is very large: the underlying chain may take values in an arbitrary space, so any process with an exponentially mixing regeneration is included, and it is hard to name a property of a psi-mixing process that forbids regeneration. A candidate invariant would be an entropy or a coding-length obstruction, but psi-mixing already forces exponential decay of all the coefficients and gives no room for such an obstruction.
attempt.key_identity: Instantaneous functions of Harris recurrent chains are exactly the processes with an i.i.d. regeneration-block decomposition.

title: Prescribing the phi-mixing coefficients exactly
statement: Suppose (b_1, b_2, b_3, ...) is an arbitrary nonincreasing sequence of numbers in [0,1]. Does there exist a strictly stationary sequence X = (X_k, k in Z) with phi(n) = b_n for every n >= 1? The source notes that the known phi-mixing constructions leave an arbitrarily small window in the specification, and that it is not even known whether there is a strictly stationary sequence with 1 > phi(1) = phi(2) > 0 = phi(3).
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 as for D0030; no exactness theorem for phi found in the later literature. The residual question (the sub-question stated in the source) has no evidence of resolution. Note the finding recorded in the attempt: the literal general form is refuted by a result quoted elsewhere in the same survey.

attempt.method: Check the literal statement against the constraints on phi already recorded in the same survey before attempting any construction.
attempt.result: The literal general form of Question 7 is FALSE, and the counterexample is one line from the survey's own text. On PDF p. 18 the source quotes, from [43, Theorem 22.14], the following for a strictly stationary sequence with NO ergodicity assumption: 'If phi(n) < 1/2 for some n >= 1, then X is phi-mixing', i.e. phi(n) -> 0. Take b_n = 1/4 for every n: it is nonincreasing and lies in [0,1], but any stationary X with phi(1) = 1/4 has phi(n) -> 0, so phi(n) = 1/4 for all n is impossible. More generally no nonincreasing sequence that drops below 1/2 without converging to 0 is realisable, and Theorem 4.1(3)(c) adds that for an ergodic-theoretically mixing sequence either phi(n) -> 0 or phi(n) = 1 for all n. So the realisable set of phi-sequences is strictly smaller than all nonincreasing [0,1]-sequences, and the substantive residual problem is to CHARACTERISE it. The source's own sub-question (is 1 > phi(1) = phi(2) > 0 = phi(3) realisable?) is not touched by these constraints, since phi(3) = 0 makes X 2-dependent and phi(1) may exceed 1/2.
attempt.obstruction: Characterising the realisable phi-sequences is where I stop. The constraints above are necessary; I have no further necessary conditions and no matching construction. The known constructions (Kesten-O'Brien and its descendants) prescribe alpha, rho and rho* exactly (Theorem 4.5 of the source) but only prescribe phi up to an arbitrarily small window, because phi is a supremum of conditional probabilities and the cutting-and-stacking constructions control measures of sets, not conditional probabilities uniformly over the past. That uniformity is the wall.
attempt.key_identity: Bradley [43, Thm 22.14] as quoted in the source: for strictly stationary X, phi(n) < 1/2 for some n implies phi(n) -> 0. Hence b_n = 1/4 for all n is unrealisable.

title: Spectral characterisation of r*(n) -> 0 for weakly stationary sequences
statement: What condition on a spectral density function is necessary and sufficient for a complex, centred, weakly stationary (CCWS) random sequence to satisfy r*(n) -> 0 as n -> infinity? (Theorem 6.5 of the source characterises the conjunction 'r*(1) < 1 and r*(n) -> 0' as the existence of a continuous positive spectral density; the question is what r*(n) -> 0 alone corresponds to.)
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 as for D0030. The survey 'Szego's Theorem and its Probabilistic Descendants' (arXiv:1108.0368, Simon) appeared in the search and treats the spectral theory of the linear dependence coefficients, but from the title and context it does not give the r*-characterisation asked here. No evidence of resolution.

attempt.method: Isolate what dropping the hypothesis r*(1) < 1 costs. Theorem 6.5 shows continuity and positivity of the spectral density f is equivalent to r*(1) < 1 together with r*(n) -> 0; so the question is which spectral densities give r*(n) -> 0 with r*(1) = 1.
attempt.result: The residual class can be described structurally, which is the content of this attempt. r*(1) = 1 means some finite interlaced pair of index sets at distance 1 already has maximal correlation 1, which for a CCWS sequence means the closed linear spans of two such families of variables touch at angle zero; this is a degeneracy of the sequence at lag 1 and is not a property of the smoothness of f but of its vanishing or of its unboundedness. Since r*(n) -> 0 is a statement about all interlaced pairs at distance n, and the operator whose norm computes r* is (a compression of) the Toeplitz operator with symbol f, the natural conjecture is: r*(n) -> 0 holds iff f is the sum of a continuous positive function and a function whose Toeplitz operator is compact on the relevant subspaces, i.e. iff f has continuous positive part with the singular set concentrated on a set that becomes invisible to interlaced blocks at large separation. Concretely I expect the answer to be: r*(n) -> 0 iff f = g h with g continuous and positive and log h in a Sarason-type space (VMO-like), which is the standard shape of the answers for r(n) and zeta(n).
attempt.obstruction: The wall is that r* is a supremum over interlaced index sets of arbitrarily many blocks, so it is not the norm of a single Toeplitz or Hankel operator but a supremum of norms of compressions to arbitrarily complicated subspaces. All the classical spectral characterisations (Helson-Sarason for rho, Kolmogorov-Rozanov for the linear coefficients) reduce to a single Hankel operator, and that reduction is unavailable here.
attempt.key_identity: Theorem 6.5 characterises 'r*(1) < 1 and r*(n) -> 0' as continuous positive spectral density; the residual class is the r*(1) = 1 degeneracy.

title: Spectral characterisation of rho*-mixing for stationary Gaussian sequences
statement: What condition on a spectral density is necessary and sufficient for a stationary Gaussian sequence to be rho*-mixing?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 as for D0030 and D0036; the Gaussian rho-mixing characterisation (Kolmogorov-Rozanov, Helson-Sarason, Ibragimov) is classical and appears in the search results, but no rho* analogue was found. No evidence of resolution.

attempt.method: Use the Gaussian reduction. For a stationary Gaussian sequence, rho for any pair of sigma-fields generated by families of the variables equals the maximal correlation of the corresponding Gaussian subspaces, so rho*(n) equals the supremum over interlaced index sets at distance n of the cosine of the angle between the two closed linear spans. So the problem is purely a question about the geometry of the Toeplitz operator with symbol f.
attempt.result: The Gaussian case therefore reduces to exactly the same operator-theoretic problem as Question 8 (D0036), which is a structural observation worth recording: for Gaussian sequences, rho*(n) = r*(n), so Questions 8 and 9 of the source are literally the same problem restricted to Gaussian sequences, and any solution of one gives the other in that class. The classical rho-answer is Helson-Sarason: rho(n) -> 0 iff f = |P|^2 exp(u + v-tilde) with u, v real continuous and P a polynomial with no zeros in the open disc; the natural rho* conjecture drops the polynomial factor and demands f = exp(u + v-tilde) with u continuous and v continuous (no zeros allowed at all), which matches Theorem 6.5 of the source in the direction where both are known.
attempt.obstruction: Same wall as D0036: rho* is a supremum over arbitrarily many interlaced blocks and is not the norm of a single Hankel operator, so the Helson-Sarason machinery (which characterises the norm of one Hankel operator with symbol the conjugate function) does not apply. The known sufficient direction (continuous positive f implies rho*(n) -> 0) is Theorem 6.5; the converse requires ruling out spectral densities with a zero or a pole that is invisible to every finite interlaced configuration, and I have no argument for that.
attempt.key_identity: For Gaussian sequences rho*(n) = r*(n), so Questions 8 and 9 coincide on the Gaussian class.

title: A finite-state, half-space 1-dependent random field measurable with respect to its own tail
statement: For a given d >= 2, does there exist a nondegenerate, strictly stationary, finite-state (or even two-state) random field X = (X_k, k in Z^d) which is (a) lattice half-space 1-dependent and (b) measurable, modulo null sets, with respect to its own tail sigma-field? The source constructs such a field with real-valued, non-discrete marginals; Robert Burton asked for a finite-state version.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 as for D0030; the survey is the most recent statement located and no finite-state construction or impossibility result appeared. No evidence of resolution.

attempt.method: Ask what the real-valued construction uses that a finite alphabet does not have. Half-space 1-dependence plus tail-measurability means the field reconstructs itself from arbitrarily distant information while being nearly independent across half-space boundaries -- a reconstruction that in the real-valued construction can hide unboundedly much information in a single real coordinate.
attempt.result: The obstruction is an entropy budget, and stating it is the useful output here. In the real-valued construction each site can carry an infinite amount of information, so the tail can determine the field by encoding it in the digits of the coordinates. With a finite alphabet the entropy per site is at most log |alphabet|, and tail-measurability forces the process to have zero entropy: if the field is measurable with respect to its tail then the entropy rate must vanish, because conditional entropy given the tail is the entropy rate and it is zero. But half-space 1-dependence forces a positive entropy rate unless the field is degenerate: 1-dependence across a half-space boundary means the conditional law of a site given the far half-space is close to its unconditional law, so the entropy rate is at least the entropy of one site minus a term controlled by the dependence, which is positive for a nondegenerate finite-state field. This looks like a genuine tension and would settle the question in the NEGATIVE for finite alphabets -- but the argument as stated is not complete, see the obstruction.
attempt.obstruction: The tension above is heuristic at exactly one point: 'lattice half-space 1-dependence' as used in the source's reference [28] is a condition on two half-spaces separated by a lattice distance one, not an independence of a single site from a half-space, so it does not directly lower-bound the entropy rate of the field by the single-site entropy. Constructing the correct entropy inequality requires the technical definitions of that paper, which are not reproduced in the survey and which I did not fetch. So the honest state is: an entropy obstruction is the natural route to a negative answer, and it needs the exact definition of half-space 1-dependence to be turned into a proof.
attempt.key_identity: Tail-measurability forces zero entropy rate; a nondegenerate finite-state field with a 1-dependence across half-space boundaries should have positive entropy rate.
